subject: english-literature
title: Unreliable Narrators and Myth
welcome_lead: Modernism distrusts its tellers — and reaches for myth to organise the chaos.
meta_desc: Unreliable narration and mythic method in modernist prose at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have read modernism's two great strategies — doubt the narrator, anchor in myth.

concepts.def: Wayne Booth's term — modernist fiction (Ford's The Good Soldier) systematises narrators whose accounts cannot be trusted.
T. S. Eliot's term for Joyce's use of the Odyssey in Ulysses — myth as a way of controlling and ordering contemporary chaos.
Reference to other texts, ubiquitous in modernist literature; readers must reconstruct the network.
Eliot's doctrine — the poet's emotion is irrelevant; what matters is the verbal artefact.
Eliot's term — the set of objects and events that evoke a specific emotion.
Pound's modernist watchword — renew form and language against the dead conventions of the late nineteenth century.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Ford Madox Ford's The Good Soldier (1915) is narrated by John Dowell, who opens 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard' and proceeds to confuse and contradict himself across a decade of remembered events.

Modernist unreliability is structural, not incidental.
In his 1923 review of Ulysses, Eliot praised Joyce's use of the Odyssey as a 'mythic method' — a way of ordering modern experience by mapping it onto ancient pattern.
Pound's imperative — make it new — became modernism's banner. It echoes a Chinese inscription: the new is old renewed.
